subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer questions about a speaker
intro: When someone speaks — a teacher giving a lesson, a classmate sharing an idea, or a speaker at an event — a good listener asks questions to make sure they understand. These questions can clarify something confusing, gather more information, or dig deeper into a topic. Answering questions about a speaker's words also helps you show that you understood what was said.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Animals migrate to find better conditions.' A listener is not sure what 'migrate' means. Which clarifying question is best?
A) 'Do you like animals?'
B) 'What does it mean to migrate?'
C) 'Can we talk about something else?'

steps: A clarifying question targets something you did not understand in what the speaker said.
Option A is a personal question unrelated to the speaker's statement.
Option C changes the topic — not a clarifying question.
Option B asks the speaker to explain the specific word that was unclear: 'migrate'.
Good clarifying questions target a specific part of what the speaker said.
solution.answer: B) 'What does it mean to migrate?' This is a clarifying question that asks the speaker to explain an unclear term.

items.prompt:
A classmate says: 'The water cycle has three steps.' A listener wants more information about what those steps are. Which question gathers additional information?
A) 'Why do you like science?'
B) 'What are the three steps?'
C) 'How many steps did you say?'

steps: Option A is off topic — it asks about feelings, not about the water cycle.
Option C repeats back a number already stated — not gathering new information.
Option B directly asks for the information that was hinted at but not provided: the names of the three steps.
Questions that gather additional information ask the speaker to expand or provide details they have not yet shared.
solution.answer: B) 'What are the three steps?' This gathers additional information that the speaker mentioned but did not yet explain.

items.prompt:
A teacher says: 'Frogs are amphibians, which means they can live on land and in water.' A student asks: 'So are all amphibians frogs?' Is this a good question to deepen understanding?
A) No — it is off topic
B) Yes — it asks the teacher to clarify whether the rule works the other way around, which deepens understanding
C) No — the student should just accept what the teacher said

steps: The student is asking whether the connection is two-way: all frogs are amphibians, but are all amphibians frogs?
This is a question that deepens understanding of a concept — it explores the limits of the definition.
Asking questions that test understanding of a concept is exactly what this standard calls for.
The answer (no — salamanders and toads are also amphibians) enriches the discussion.
solution.answer: B) Yes. The student asks whether the relationship works both ways — this deepens their understanding of what 'amphibian' means.

items.prompt:
A speaker says something confusing. A listener asks: 'When you said the bees communicate by dancing, did you mean they actually move their bodies in a pattern, or is that just a saying?' Is this a good clarifying question?
A) No — it is too long
B) Yes — it asks the speaker to confirm which of two interpretations is correct, which clarifies comprehension
C) No — the listener should look it up instead

steps: This question offers two possible interpretations and asks the speaker to confirm which one is accurate.
This is an excellent form of clarification: it shows the listener was paying attention and identified an ambiguity.
Clarifying questions like this help ensure the listener understood the speaker's meaning correctly.
Length of a question does not determine its quality — clarity of purpose does.
solution.answer: B) Yes. The question asks the speaker to confirm which interpretation is correct — this is a precise and effective clarifying question.

items.prompt:
A student gives a presentation about penguins. After the presentation, a classmate asks: 'You mentioned penguins swim very fast. How fast can they swim?' What kind of question is this?
A) A question that changes the topic
B) A question that gathers additional information the speaker did not fully provide
C) A question that disagrees with the speaker

steps: The classmate is asking for a specific detail (the speed) that the speaker mentioned but did not quantify.
This is a question that gathers additional information — the speaker said 'very fast' but did not give a number.
The question stays on topic (penguins, swimming speed) and asks for more precise information.
It does not disagree with the speaker — it asks for elaboration.
solution.answer: B) A question that gathers additional information. The speaker said penguins swim 'very fast' but did not say how fast — this question asks for the specific detail.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'You should always wash your hands before eating.' A listener wants to understand why. Which question is best?
A) 'Do you like food?'
B) 'Why is it important to wash hands before eating?'
C) 'When did you first learn this?'
items.hint: A good question targets the specific part of the statement you want to understand better. What is missing from the speaker's statement?

steps: The speaker stated a rule but did not explain the reason.
Option A is off topic.
Option C asks about the speaker personally — not about the information.
Option B asks for the reason behind the rule, which deepens understanding.
Asking 'why' is a great way to deepen understanding of a statement.
solution.answer: B) 'Why is it important to wash hands before eating?' This asks for the reasoning behind the statement, which deepens understanding.

items.prompt:
A classmate gives a talk about recycling and says: 'Plastic takes a long time to break down.' A listener thinks: 'How long is a long time?' Which question best gathers additional information?
A) 'Do you recycle at home?'
B) 'How long does it actually take for plastic to break down?'
C) 'Is plastic the only thing that takes a long time?'
items.hint: The listener is curious about the specific number or time frame behind 'a long time'. Which question asks for that?

steps: The speaker used a vague phrase — 'a long time' — without specifying how long.
Option A is personal and off topic.
Option C is related but asks a different question about other materials.
Option B directly asks for the specific information that 'a long time' glossed over.
Questions that ask for specific details make vague statements more concrete.
solution.answer: B) 'How long does it actually take for plastic to break down?' This gathers the specific detail that was vague in the speaker's statement.

items.prompt:
A teacher explains: 'Abraham Lincoln was born in a log cabin in Kentucky.' A student asks: 'What is a log cabin?' Is this a good clarifying question?
A) No — the student should already know what a log cabin is
B) Yes — asking for the meaning of an unfamiliar term is a good clarifying question
C) No — log cabins are not important
items.hint: A clarifying question targets something you do not fully understand. Is asking for a definition a valid form of clarification?

steps: If the student does not know what a log cabin is, asking is the right response.
Asking 'what is a log cabin?' targets an unfamiliar term used by the speaker.
This is exactly the kind of question that helps clarify comprehension.
There is no expectation that listeners already know every word — asking is always appropriate.
solution.answer: B) Yes. Asking for the meaning of an unfamiliar term ('what is a log cabin?') is a good clarifying question.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Exercise is important for your health.' After the talk, a student asks: 'Could you give an example of a type of exercise that is especially good for kids?' What is the purpose of this question?
A) To disagree with the speaker
B) To gather additional information with a specific example
C) To change the topic to a different health topic
items.hint: Asking for an example is one way to deepen understanding. What is the student trying to learn?

steps: The speaker made a general statement: exercise is important.
The student wants a SPECIFIC example, especially one relevant to kids.
Asking for an example is a form of gathering additional information.
The question stays on topic (exercise, health) and asks for more detail.
This deepens understanding by making the general statement more concrete.
solution.answer: B) To gather additional information with a specific example. The student wants the speaker to make the general statement more concrete.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads aloud and then asks students if they have questions. A student asks: 'You said the sun is a star — but it looks much bigger than stars at night. Why does it look so different?' What type of question is this?
A) A question that does not relate to what the teacher said
B) A question that deepens understanding by asking for a reason that explains something seemingly contradictory
C) A question that disagrees with the teacher
items.hint: The student noticed what seems like a contradiction between two things they know. Is asking about that contradiction a way to deepen understanding?

steps: The student noticed an apparent contradiction: the teacher said the sun is a star, but it looks different from night-time stars.
Asking WHY the sun looks different is asking the teacher to explain something that deepens understanding of the concept.
This is not disagreement — it accepts that the sun is a star but asks for the explanation of the apparent difference.
Questions that explore 'why does this seem contradictory?' are high-level comprehension questions.
solution.answer: B) A question that deepens understanding. The student is asking for an explanation of something that seems contradictory — why does the sun look so different from other stars? (Answer: it is much closer.)
